subject: Anthropology
title: High-Altitude Adaptation
description: A fast breakdown of High-Altitude Adaptation for builders.

hook.text: At 14,000 feet, most people gasp for air. Tibetans breathe normally. Their genes have adapted to thin air.

buildup.text: Tibetans carry a variant of the EPAS1 gene that prevents overproduction of red blood cells at high altitude.

discovery.text: Andean peoples adapted differently — with larger lungs and more hemoglobin. Same problem, different genetic solutions.

twist.text: The Tibetan EPAS1 variant came from Denisovans. Ancient interbreeding gave a survival edge thousands of years later.

climax.text: High-altitude adaptation shows evolution in action. Humans haven't stopped evolving — the environment still selects.

punchline.text: Evolution didn't stop — it just got local.

quiz.question: Where did Tibetans get the EPAS1 gene variant?

details.summary: Populations living at high altitudes for thousands of years — Tibetans, Andean peoples, Ethiopian highlanders — evolved distinct biological adaptations to low oxygen. These include increased hemoglobin efficiency, higher lung capacity, and genetic variants that prevent altitude sickness.
details.whyItMatters: High-altitude adaptation demonstrates that human evolution is ongoing and geographically diverse. Different populations evolved different solutions to the same environmental challenge.
takeaways: Multiple populations evolved distinct adaptations to high altitude
Tibetans, Andeans, and Ethiopians each adapted differently
This shows human evolution is ongoing and finds multiple solutions

faq.question: How do Tibetan high-altitude adaptations work?
faq.answer: Tibetans carry a variant of the EPAS1 gene, inherited from Denisovan ancestors, that prevents overproduction of red blood cells at altitude. Unlike Andeans who increase hemoglobin levels.

faq.question: How quickly did high-altitude adaptations evolve?
faq.answer: Tibetans colonized the plateau within the last 10,000 to 15,000 years, making their adaptations among the fastest documented evolutionary changes in humans. This demonstrates that strong selection pressures — low oxygen at extreme altitude — can drive rapid genetic change in human populations.
